texts.city: You have solid savings and income but negative yearly cash flow and tight near-term cash needs.
texts.strength: You save $43,000 a year and capture your full $7,000 employer match.

cashflow.building: Your income is being asked to cover too many goals at once.
cashflow.plain: You bring in $180,000 a year before taxes. After taxes and spending, your cash flow is -$8,336 a year.
cashflow.standard: You save $43,000 a year (including a $7,000 employer match) but still run a net cash flow of -$8,336 a year. Your income is $180,000 and your expenses are $66,000 a year, with taxes of $40,664. That negative flow means retirement, near-term goals, and a cash cushion are competing for the same dollars.

cushion.building: Your accessible cash is well below the reserve plus near-term goals.
cushion.plain: You have $30,000 available now, which covers about 3.2 months of expenses. Adding your January 2027 home and vacation needs pushes the cash target to $163,330 to $172,636.
cushion.standard: Accessible cash is $30,000 and covers 3.2 months of essential expenses against a recommended reserve of $46,530 to $55,836. The January 2027 home payment of $113,300 plus a $3,500 vacation raise the cash target to $163,330 to $172,636, leaving you with 0 months covered after setting those aside.

retirement.building: Retiring at 58 leaves a substantial retirement-account gap and money runs out before the plan ends.
retirement.plain: You aim to retire at 58 but savings run out at age 85, leaving $32,439 of planned spending unpaid. Social Security covers about 34% of your $89,649 yearly need.
retirement.standard: At retirement you have a net worth of $1,535,457 with $1,071,095 liquid, but savings and investments run out at age 85 leaving $32,439 unpaid. Guaranteed income averages $30,036 a year and covers 34% of the $89,649 yearly retirement spending need, so $59,613 a year must come from savings. The retirement-account gap is $1,177,586 in today's dollars, and closing it projects to require $20,231 more per year.

debt.building: You have manageable total debt, but the 20% credit card is expensive for its size.
debt.plain: Total debt is $28,500 with payments of $11,400 a year. Your Amex Platinum balance is $3,500 at 20% interest and is projected to be paid off by July 2028 if $200 a month continues.
debt.standard: Debt totals $28,500, about 15.83% of your $180,000 income, and debt payments are $11,400 a year. The Amex Platinum at $3,500 carries 20% interest and, at $200 a month, is on track to be paid off by July 2028. Your housing and debt payments share of income is 25.37%, below the 36% threshold.

protection.building: Your life insurance and umbrella coverage are far below recommended levels.
protection.plain: You have $180,000 of life insurance while the plan recommends $900,000 to $1,800,000. You have no umbrella liability cover, but the recommendation is $1,000,000.
protection.standard: Life insurance is $180,000 versus a recommended $900,000 to $1,800,000, leaving a large shortfall. You have no umbrella cover though the plan recommends $1,000,000. Because your $180,000 income is the only household income, this protection gap matters for covering debts like your $15,000 car loan, $10,000 student loan, and $3,500 credit card.

investments.building: Most wealth is investable but your current stock mix lags your Growth target.
investments.plain: You hold $145,000 of invested savings, which is 58.7% of $247,000 total assets. Your current mix is 59% stocks versus a 67% target for Growth.
investments.standard: Invested savings are $145,000 (58.7% of $247,000 total assets) and 73.5% of assets are in stocks versus a 98% target mix for the chosen horizon. Your recorded account holdings include VTI $60,000, VWO $22,000, SCHD $20,000, and SCHP $18,000. The plan notes rebuilding your emergency reserve and paying the $3,500 credit card before adding to retirement, and suggests you could add up to $7,500 to your 401(k) or $4,500 to a Roth IRA within the limits noted.

score.building: Your overall score is 26, driven down by liquidity and protection gaps.
score.plain: The plan score is 26 out of 100, in the critical band. Savings and cash flow scored 0/25 and insurance and protection scored 4/20.
score.standard: Your score is 26, with savings and cash flow 0/25, debt 8/10, investments 11/25, liquidity 4/20, and insurance 4/20. The plan highlights that adding $1M of umbrella cover would move the score from 26 to 31.

assumptions.building: The projection relies on a set of specific assumptions about income, returns, and timing.
assumptions.plain: The plan assumes you retire at 58 and the plan runs to age 91. It assumes prices rise 3% a year and investments grow 7.76% a year.
assumptions.standard: Key assumptions include Michael retires at 58, the plan runs to age 91, prices rise 3% annually, investments grow 7.76% annually, salary of $180,000 continues until 2047, and Social Security starts in 2056. The plan also assumes a $3,500 annual vacation and a $550,000 home purchase in 2027.

m0.title: Get an umbrella quote
m0.why: The plan flags no umbrella cover while recommending $1,000,000 to improve your protection score.
steps: Search for umbrella insurance quotes online or call your current insurer.
Ask for a $1,000,000 policy option to compare cost and coverage.
Compare premiums to your monthly budget before deciding.

quiz.q: Why does the plan suggest an umbrella policy?
options: To meet the recommended $1,000,000 liability shield
To replace your life insurance entirely
quiz.explain: The plan recommends $1,000,000 of umbrella liability cover because you currently have none and it would improve protection.

m1.title: Review your withdrawal plan
m1.why: Lowering withdrawals to reach the sustainable band is shown to raise the plan score and protect longevity.
steps: Open your retirement projection or account statements.
Check current withdrawal assumptions against the plan's sustainable band.
Consider how reducing withdrawals to $10,300 a year fits your budget.

quiz.q: What withdrawal level does the plan say reaches the sustainable band?
quiz.explain: The plan states cutting withdrawals to $10,300/year reaches the sustainable band.

m2.title: Compare your stock mix
m2.why: The plan recommends raising growth allocation toward the glide to match your Growth profile and improve the score.
steps: Pull your current account allocation from statements.
Compare your 59% stock mix to the 67% target in the plan.
If you decide to adjust, move toward the glide within your accounts.

quiz.q: What stock mix target does the plan set for your Growth profile?
quiz.explain: The plan's target mix for Growth is 67% stocks, while your current mix is 59%.
